Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Assess the complex anatomy of the distal femur and the deforming forces that affect distal
femur fracture reduction.
Determine distal femur fracture mechanisms of injury and the appropriate assessment and
documentation of associated injuries.
Compare methods of surgical management of distal femur fractures and apply basic fracture
principles.
Avoid pitfalls and complications associated with distal femur fracture fixation.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
The distal end of the femur traditionally encompasses the lower one-third of the femur.

The distal femur extends 7 to 15 cm from the joint surface proximally.
This lesson reviews fractures that involve the supracondylar (metaphyseal) and intercondylar
(epiphyseal) areas of the distal femur. Pertinent anatomy, injury assessment, and various
treatment options are discussed.
Epidemiology
Distal femur fractures account for 3% to 6% of all femur fractures.
Distal femur fractures have a bimodal distribution.
The incidence is higher in young, healthy males (often from high-energy trauma) and elderly
females with osteopenia (from low-energy mechanisms of injury).
Elsoe et al1 reported distal femur fractures as a classic fragility fracture, with a mean patient
age of 67.3 years and most fractures (83%) occurring in women.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The supracondylar (metaphyseal) region of the distal femur transitions from the cylindrical
shaft to the trapezoidal metaphysis.
The narrow side of the trapezoid is anterior.
The distal femur is composed mainly of cancellous bone.
Mechanical axis (axis that extends from the center of the femoral head to the center of the
ankle joint): subtends an angle 3° from vertical
Anatomic axis (axis that extends the length of the central portion of the bone): subtends an
angle 6° valgus to the mechanical axis
The distal femur is in physiologic valgus of approximately 9°.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
In referring to the axes of the lower extremity anatomic axis and a mechanical axis
exist2 (Figure 1). The femur and its axes do not superimpose. The mechanical axis
begins from the center of the femoral head and ends at the central portion of the
tibial plafond. This mechanical axis creates approximately 3° of varus in reference to
the vertical axis. The anatomic axis begins in the piriformis fossa at the proximal
aspect and ends in the central aspect of the intercondylar notch distally. The anatomic

2/35

axis is approximately 6° lateral to the vertical axis and 3° lateral to the mechanical
axis.
Figure 1 Illustration of a femur shows the anatomic axis and the mechanical axis of
the lower extremity. (Modified with permission from Helfet DL: Fractures of the distal
femur, in Browner BD, Jupiter JB, Levine AM, Trafton PG, eds: Skeletal Trauma.
Philadelphia, PA, Saunders, 1992, pp 1643-1683.)

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084

Osteology
The medial condyle extends more distal than the lateral condyle.
In the axial plane, the lateral cortex slopes approximately 10° lateral to medial.
In the axial plane, the medial cortex slopes approximately 25° medial to lateral.
The posterior halves of both condyles are posterior to the posterior cortex of femoral
shaft3(Figure 2).
Figure 2 Illustration shows the axial geometry of the distal femur. Note the lateral slope of 10°
and the 25° slope of the medial femoral condyle. Pre-contoured locking plates account for this
slope. Bicortical screws used in the anterior half of the distal femur, which appear to be the
correct length on an AP radiograph, often are too long and encroach on the medical collateral
ligament. (Reproduced with permission from Beltran MJ, Gary JL, Collinge CA: Management of
distal femur fractures with modern plates and nails: State of the art. J Orthop Trauma
2015;29[4]:165-172.)
Vascular Anatomy
The femoral artery in the distal portion of the thigh runs through the adductor canal.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
4/35

It is in close proximity to the medial cortex of the distal end of the femur as it passes through
to the posterior compartment approximately 10 cm above the knee joint.
With high-energy injuries, gunshot injuries, or open distal femoral injuries, the femoral artery
is at substantial risk of injury.
With associated ligament disruptions of the knee (especially a posterior dislocation), the
popliteal artery is at great risk of injury (as high as 40% in some series).
A potential for popliteal artery injury exists in patients with considerable displacement of
fracture fragments.
Ankle-brachial index (ABI) should be performed if concern for vascular injury exists.
Angiography is indicated if the ABI is less than 0.9
An ABI higher than 0.9 is associated with a 99% negative predictive value for popliteal
artery injury.
An ABI less than 0.9 is 97% specific and 95% sensitive for the diagnosis of a major arterial
injury.

Vascular Anatomy
The vascular anatomy of the distal femur and the knee is complex, with a robust
anastomotic network. The popliteal artery is the direct continuation of the femoral
artery at the adductor hiatus. Passing to the back of the knee at the hiatus, the artery
descends through the popliteal space with a slight mediolateral inclination and ends
at the lower border of the popliteal muscle by dividing into the anterior and posterior
tibial arteries. The artery is deeper in the popliteal space than the corresponding vein
and the tibial nerve, lying in the intercondylar fossa of the femur and against the
posterior capsule of the knee joint. The popliteal artery gives off five genicular
branches: the lateral superior genicular artery, medial superior genicular artery,
middle genicular artery, lateral inferior genicular artery, and the medial inferior
genicular artery.4 On the medial aspect of the distal femur, the mean distance from
adductor tubercle to femoral artery is approximately 23.2 cm, 18.8 cm, and 14.3 cm at
the level of the anterior, midsagittal, and posterior femur, respectively. During
dissection deep to the vastus medialis, the descending genicular artery and its
branches to the vastus medialis are identified5 (Figure 3).

The popliteal artery lies directly behind the distal femoral metaphysis. Therefore, it
may be at risk during anteroposterior screw insertion. (Reproduced with permission
from Besselaar A, Green D, Howard A: Neurovascular anatomy. AO Surgery Reference.
Available at:

trauma/femoral-shaft/further-reading/neurovascular-anatomy#neurovascular-

Sciatic nerve
Common peroneal nerve
Tibial nerve

Posterior cruciate ligament
Lateral collateral ligament
Medial collateral ligament (Figure 4)
Associated ligamentous disruption after distal femur fracture occurs in approximately 20% of
patients. Ligamentous injuries cannot be accurately diagnosed until after fracture fixation
because of bony instability.

Musculature

Anterior femoral muscles: sartorius, quadriceps femoris (combined rectus femoris and
vastus muscles), and the articularis genus muscles.
Medial femoral muscles: gracilis, pectineus, adductor longus/brevis/magnus, and obturator
externus
Posterior femoral muscles: hamstring group (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and
biceps femoris) and ischiocondylar portion of the adductor magnus (Figure 5)

Figure 5 Illustrations of the leg show the hip and thigh muscles. Anterior view illustrations of a
right leg show the superficial (A) and deep (B) pelvic and thigh muscles. C, Posterior view
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
10/35

illustration of a right leg shows the pelvic and thigh muscles. The large and powerful muscles
of the hip that move the femur generally originate on the pelvic girdle and insert into the
femur. The muscles that move the lower leg typically originate on the femur and insert into the
bones of the knee joint. The anterior muscles of the femur extend the lower leg but also aid in
flexing the thigh. The posterior muscles of the femur flex the lower leg but also aid in
extending the thigh. A combination of gluteal and thigh muscles also adduct, abduct, and
rotate the thigh and the lower leg. (Reproduced with permission from Betts JG, Young KA, Wise
JA, et al: Appendicular muscles of the pelvic girdle and lower limbs, in Anatomy and Physiology.
Houston, TX, OpenStax, 2013.) 

Musculature
The deforming forces of the distal femur after a fracture are related to the pull of the
muscular attachments about the knee 4. The origin of the gastrocnemius
characteristically pulls the distal fracture fragment into extension, resulting in apex
posterior angulation. The adductor musculature in combination with the mechanical
axis of the extremity shortens and pulls the fracture into varus. In patients who have
more severe fractures with intercondylar involvement, rotational malalignment of the
condyles relative to each other is observed in the frontal plane, which is the result of
their muscular attachments.7 Successful fracture reduction requires an
understanding of these deforming forces, overcoming them, and resisting them via
fixation.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Fractures involving the supracondylar femur often result from the same high-energy
mechanisms of injury associated with fractures of the femoral shaft.
Low-energy mechanisms of injury, such as minor falls, are common in the older population.
Risk Factors
Risk factors include the following:1
Increasing age 1

Female sex (increased age)
Male sex (younger patients)
Osteoporosis
Total knee arthroplasty
Associated Injuries
Depends on the mechanism of injury
Patella fracture
Associated femoral shaft fracture
Proximal femur/acetabular fracture
Injury Classification
The Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation classification is the universally accepted
system for classifying injuries of the distal femur.
Type A fractures are extra-articular injuries.
Type B fractures are partially articular and involve a single condyle.
Type C fractures are complete articular, intercondylar, or bicondylar intra-articular injuries
with varying degrees of comminution (Figure 6).
SEND FEEDBACK

Figure 6 Illustration shows the Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation classification
of distal femur fractures. (Reproduced with permission from Kanakeshwar RB, Arun KC,
Dheenadayalan J: Classification of distal femur fractures and their clinical relevance. Trauma
International 2016;2(1):3-6.)
Mechanism of Injury
Mechanical falls
Higher energy mechanisms of injury (eg, motorcycle collision, motor vehicle collision, fall from
height)
Axial load to a flexed knee


Mechanism of Injury
Fractures that occur in elderly patients typically result from low-energy mechanisms of
injury, such as falls. In the younger patient population, these fractures result from higher
energy mechanisms of injury. These may result from a direct load to a flexed knee
during a motor vehicle accident, motorcycle accident, or fall from height. These fractures
often have intra-articular extension because of their higher energy. A female
preponderance exists in the older patient population, and a male preponderance exists
in the younger patient population.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Evaluation
Mechanism of injury
Identify area of pain, swelling, and deformity
Neurovascular structures lie close to these fractures; therefore, neurovascular status should
be assessed thoroughly.
The skin should be examined closely for open wounds.
In elderly patients, preexisting medical conditions and degenerative knee joint disease should
be considered.
Assess and document pre-injury ambulation status.

Clinical Evaluation
In patients with a higher energy mechanism of injury, Advanced Trauma Life Support
protocol must be followed. A thorough examination of the entire patient is performed,
and all areas of pain, bruising, and bleeding are documented. In addition, a
neurovascular examination is performed on all extremities. In the geriatric patient
population, the entire patient is examined, and a thorough skin examination is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
14/35

performed. Open fractures should be diagnosed, and skin ulcerations that may have
resulted from prolonged recumbency should be noted.
Patient History
Mechanism of injury
Specific area of pain
Medical comorbidities
Pre-injury ambulatory status
History of knee pain
History of surgery to the affected extremity

Patient History
The patient’s mechanism of injury should be detailed, and a thorough medical history
should be obtained. Patient comorbidities, especially in elderly patients, can provide
insight into bone health or other metabolic/pathologic processes that may have
contributed to fracture. In addition, elements in the patient history may need to be
optimized or managed before surgical management.
Physical Examination
Inspection
Palpation

Physical Examination
Areas of tenderness, swelling, and ecchymosis of the extremity must be identified and
documented. This requires radiographic examination to identify other injuries. Overt
deformity, such as varus or valgus deformity of the knee, will be observed. Knee
effusions should be identified because they may be present in patients with intra-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
15/35

articular involvement. Physical examination should identify persistently bleeding wounds
in the area of the supracondylar region because the incidence of open distal femur
fracture in as high as 5% to 10%.7 Range of motion, strength, and stability examinations
about the knee generally are deferred in patients with an acute fracture.
Neurovascular Examination
Vascular evaluation
Potential for injury to popliteal artery if considerable fracture displacement is present
ABI should be performed if concern for vascular injury exists.
Angiography is indicated if the ABI is less than 0.9
ABI higher than 0.9 is associated with a 99% negative predictive value.
ABI less than 0.9 is 97% specific and 95% sensitive for the diagnosis of major arterial injury.
Neurologic evaluation
Peroneal nerve function
Sensory disruption

Neurovascular Examination
The neurovascular examination is a critical aspect of the patient evaluation. High-energy
distal femur fractures can represent a form of a knee dislocation. These variants may be
associated with a risk of popliteal artery injury in as many as 40% of patients;8 therefore,
prompt diagnosis and management are paramount to prevent catastrophic sequelae.
The neurologic examination is important to ensure no injury to the common peroneal
nerve exists because this may be indicative of knee dislocation.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
AP and lateral radiographs of the distal femur are standard views.

9/3/26, 4:14 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
16/35

Radiographic evaluation of the ipsilateral lower extremity should be considered because of the
risk of associated injuries.
Traction radiographs are helpful but may be too uncomfortable for the patient.
Computed Tomography
Oblique radiographs may provide additional details regarding intercondylar anatomy;
however, CT often eliminates the need for these additional radiographic views.
CT provides details regarding intra-articular involvement and can be used to identify coronal
plane deformities via reconstruction images.
CT should be obtained after fracture/extremity length restored. CT can be performed after
external fixation of length-unstable fractures or after splinting of length-stable fractures.
May include CT angiography to assess vasculature about the knee/fracture

Computed Tomography
If doubt exists with regard to intra-articular involvement, CT may aid in the detection of a
nondisplaced or minimally displaced fracture; may aid in understanding of complex
fracture patterns; and may aid in planning the surgical approach, especially for minimally
invasive techniques.9
. CT also is imperative to diagnose an associated coronal plane Hoffa fragment, which
typically requires stabilization independent of the articular block (Figure 7).

Figure 7 Sagittal (top), axial (middle), and coronal (bottom) CT scans of a knee show a
Hoffa fracture of the lateral condyle. (Reproduced with permission from Soni A, Kansay
R, Gupta S, Malhotra A: In situ fixation of symptomatic fibrous non-union Hoffa fracture:
A case report. Malays Orthop J 2019;13[1]:57-59.)
Differential Diagnosis
Knee dislocation
Tibial plateau fracture
Patellar dislocation
Management
Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
18/35

Nonsurgical management is indicated only for nondisplaced distal femur fractures.
Nonsurgical management of displaced supracondylar and intercondylar femur fractures
generally is associated with poor results and should be reserved for patients who represent an
unacceptable surgical treatment risk.
Indications
Stable fractures
Nondisplaced fractures that pose no risk to the soft tissues
Patient is unsafe for surgical treatment
The fracture is amenable to immediate hip and knee range of motion
Patient is can adhere to non–weight-bearing status and can be mobilized without risk
Contraindications
Unstable fractures
Fractures with displacement
Fractures that pose a risk to the soft tissues
Patient cannot adhere to weight-bearing restrictions
Techniques/Procedures
Hinged knee brace to control varus/valgus stress
Skeletal traction for 6 to 8 weeks followed by functional bracing
Nonsurgical management via traction followed by bracing is extremely rare and poorly
tolerated.
Outcomes
Patients with a distal femur fracture who undergo nonsurgical treatment have an increased
risk for:
Deep vein thrombosis (despite Coumadin therapy)
Urinary tract and pulmonary infection
Pressure sores
Nonunion
Malunion
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
19/35

Pin tract infection
Mean length of stay is 9 weeks after nonsurgical management.
Surgical management allows for early range of motion and mobilization.

Outcomes
Nonsurgical management is associated with unfavorable outcomes10. It is reserved for
patients who have extreme medical comorbidities that make surgical treatment
impossible. Nonsurgical management requires prolonged periods of immobilization. This
joint immobilization may lead to adhesions, fibrosis, and scarring of the quadriceps
musculature. After sufficient healing, the patient can be transitioned to a cast brace that
allows for knee range of motion. Good to excellent results are obtained in 53% of the
surgical managed distal femur fractures and 31% of nonsurgically managed distal femur
fractures.
Surgical Management
Temporary stabilization
Skeletal traction
Closed injuries
Patients too unstable to undergo immediate surgical stabilization
External fixation
Temporary measure to restore length, alignment, and stability
Unstable patients
Soft tissues not amenable to surgical incisions and internal fixation
Fractures requiring serial débridement
Definitive fixation
Plate fixation
Typically, fixed angle fixation
In fixed angle fixation, the normal distal femoral angle can be maintained with the use of a
single, laterally placed implant.
Locking and non-locking screws can be used to optimize fracture strain and promote a
biomechanically favorable environment.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
20/35

Targeting jigs allow for less soft-tissue dissection during the placement of proximal screws
through the plate.
Plates can be contoured to match the patient’s bony anatomy.
A combination of medial and lateral plate fixation can be used to increase the
biomechanical stability of the construct.11
Dual plating may potentially allow early weight bearing.
Intramedullary nail fixation
Allows for immediate weight bearing in patients with extra-articular or simple articular
fractures
Creates medial column support
Can be used in combination with a laterally based plate to resist varus malalignment
Distal femur replacement
Unstable periprosthetic fractures
Highly comminuted fractures in elderly patients with impaired healing ability (ie,
chemotherapy, longstanding corticosteroid use)
Pre-existing symptomatic degenerative arthritis in low-demand patients.

Surgical Management
The goal of surgical management is to create a construct that is biomechanically stable
to allow for early mobilization and joint range of motion, which can be accomplished
with a combination of a plate, a nail, or arthroplasty. Regardless of the selected method,
fracture fixation requires biologically sound dissection to ensure preservation of the
periosteum and the soft-tissue attachments.
Indications
Unstable fractures
Intra-articular fractures
Fractures with displacement
Fractures that pose a risk to the soft tissues
Patient cannot adhere to weight-bearing restrictions
Patient cannot mobilize safely while adhering to precautions
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
21/35


Indications
Surgical fixation is the preferred treatment options for distal femur fractures. In the
elderly population, failure to fix these fractures may render the patient immobile, which
may lead to extremely poor outcomes. Patients treated nonsurgically have a high risk for
deep vein thrombosis, pressure ulcers, and pneumonia, all of which contribute to
patient mortality. Surgical management affords decreased pain with patient mobility and
decreased stiffness in the hip and knee joint. Patients can transfer more easily, and the
risk of non-surgical-related complications is decreased.
Contraindications
Patients with severe medical comorbidities that cannot be optimized for surgical treatment
Techniques/Procedures
Open fractures should be managed according to open fracture management principles.
External fixators should be used until the soft tissue permits the placement of internal fixation.
Surgical tactic is dictated by the degree of articular involvement.
Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation type A fractures
Plate fixation is a viable treatment option and is associated with good results. Traditional
plating options include a dynamic condylar screw, a 95° blade plate, or a plate and screw
construct with locking screw options (most common). A dynamic condylar screw or a blade
plate requires surgical exposure of the length of the plate to allow for application.
Locked plating can be performed via a minimally invasive lateral approach to the distal
femur, exposing only the portion of the distal lateral condyle necessary to facilitate
placement of the implant (Video 1).
Retrograde intramedullary nail fixation; blocking screws can be used in patients with
spacious metaphyseal segments.
Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation type B fractures
Partial articular fractures can be managed via a buttress plate technique to create an
absolutely stable construct.
Anatomic reduction of the articular surface via direct visualization
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
22/35

Lag screw fixation of the simple articular fracture
Do not over-compress comminuted joint fractures.
Coronal plane fractures must be diagnosed (usually via CT) and managed via independent
fixation.
Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation type C fractures
Intra-articular fractures with complete dissociation between the articular block and the
metaphysis
Varying degrees of articular and metaphyseal comminution may be present.
Hybrid fixation techniques (absolute and relative stability)
Open approach to the articular surface with direct reduction and an absolutely stable
construct (lag screw fixation)
Restoration of length, alignment, and rotation of the articular block in relation to the
femoral shaft
This can be accomplished via a bridging technique.
Options for restoration of the anatomic surface to the shaft
Laterally based locked plate
Retrograde intramedullary nail
Laterally based locked plate and retrograde intramedullary nail
Laterally based locked plate and medially based plate
Intramedullary nails
Modern intramedullary nails with multiple screw options have become an effective fixation
method.
Reduction of the articular surface is performed first, followed by nail placement.
Care must be taken to place fixation so it does not block the path of the intramedullary nail.
Supracondylar fracture after total knee arthroplasty
Evaluation of the stability of the prosthesis is important. If the prosthesis is stable, then the
fixation strategy can be planned.
If the implant is stable, then the surgical treatment option must be selected.
Lateral locked plating and retrograde intramedullary nailing are viable treatment options.
Lateral locked plating
Must be placed on the anterolateral surface of the distal femur to prevent medial
translation of the articular component.
Ensure the plate and implant are not in direct contact so metal debris and corrosion are
not created
Retrograde intramedullary nailing
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
23/35

Must identify the type of implant present
If the implant has an open box, then intramedullary nail fixation is an option.
The starting point during retrograde intramedullary nailing in a patient with a total knee
arthroplasty implant is more posterior and may result in a flexion deformity through the
fracture.
Video 1 Ricci WM: Locked plating of distal femur fractures, from Horwitz DS, Watson JT, eds:
Standing Room Only: Tactics for Orthopaedic Trauma [DVD]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2013.

Techniques/Procedures
In selecting a surgical tactic, an understanding of the fracture and the mode of desired
healing are essential. The two modes of healing are primary and secondary bone
healing. Primary bone healing is healing without callus, which essentially is a remodeling
of the bone and fracture until such time that the fracture lines will fade. Primary bone
healing is accomplished by creating absolute stability at the fracture site. Techniques
such as lag screws, compression plating, and buttress plating will create an absolutely
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:14 PM
AAOS | Fractures of the Distal Femur
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001084
24/35

stable construct. Absolute stability is most commonly used for management of the
articular fracture. A surgical approach is performed to expose the fracture, which is then
reduced under direct visualization and stabilized. Secondary bone healing is healing with
fracture callus. Through micromotion of fracture fragments, callus formation occurs,
which will ultimately remodel and form cortical bone. Secondary bone healing is
accomplished by creating a relatively stable construct. Examples include external
fixation, bridge plating, and intramedullary nail fixation. This technique can be used for
the management of comminuted segments in the metaphyseal region of the distal
femur. Indirect reduction techniques (traction) are used to restore the length, alignment,
and rotation of the fracture, which is then stabilized. No formal open approach of the
comminuted segment is necessary to preserve soft-tissue biology.12
Preoperative Planning
Obtain all imaging studies before surgical planning.
Understand all the articular fracture fragments, especially the presence of a coronal fracture
fragment.
Ensure all the necessary instruments/implants are available.
Examples of equipment that can be used
External fixation
Skeletal traction
Large distractor
Reduction clamps
Provisional fixation (ie, Kirschner wires)
2.7-/3.5-mm screws for joint fixation
Lateral locked plating system
Retrograde intramedullary nailing system
Patient Positioning
The patient can be positioned supine or laterally on a radiolucent table.
The knee should be flexed over a radiolucent triangle or a series of bumps.

Surgical Approach
For simple fractures, direct reduction with absolute stability (lag screw and neutralization
plate versus compression plate) and intramedullary nail fixation are viable surgical
treatment options.
If a retrograde intramedullary nail is being used, indirect reduction techniques are used.
These include a method of traction that can restore length, alignment, and rotation of
the fracture. After alignment has been restored, fracture fixation can be performed. If a
plate is being used, a lateral approach to the distal femur is performed, and the plate is
proximally slid onto the lateral aspect of the femur in a retrograde fashion.
In patients with a displaced intra-articular fracture, direct visualization of the intra-
articular component is necessary to ensure anatomic reduction of the joint surface.
Several approaches can be used. The first approach is a lateral parapatellar arthrotomy,
which allows for complete joint exposure, direct visualization, and placement of
independent lag screws from lateral to medial. Through this lateral parapatellar
arthrotomy, a distal femoral plate can be proximally slid in a retrograde fashion to
reduce the articular block to the shaft of the femur. This technique has been termed
transarticular reconstruction and plate osteosynthesis.13
A second approach is an extensile lateral approach to the distal femur. This approach
involves an incision over the lateral aspect of the knee and thigh, through which a lateral
parapatellar arthrotomy is created and the vastus lateralis is elevated off the
intermuscular septum of the thigh. This is a more invasive technique that requires more
soft-tissue dissection, and it may be limiting in the management of medial fractures.14

Bridging external fixation may be advantageous as a temporary measure in patients with an
open fracture or patients who have a fracture with substantial comminution or soft-tissue
compromise.
If using bridging external fixation, the external fixator pins should be placed away from the
footprint of the planned definitive fixation if possible.
Postoperative Management
Fracture fixation should be rigid enough to allow for early range of motion.
Motion can be initiated as the soft-tissue envelope allows. If concern exists regarding wound
healing, then motion should be delayed until they have stabilized.
Weight bearing is based on the amount of joint involvement/comminution, the type and
location of fixation devices, and bone quality.
Two-column support (lateral and medial fixation) may allow for earlier weight bearing.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Many pitfalls can be avoided in the management of distal femur fractures if a thorough
preoperative evaluation is performed.
Preoperative surgical planning is important to identify the key fracture fragments and to
identify all the appropriate implants and hardware that should be available.

Malunion
Despite anatomic alignment, the distal femur tends to fail and fall into varus. This occurs
more frequently in patients with considerable metaphyseal comminution and minimal
medial bony apposition. Techniques, including the addition of medial plate fixation and
combined intramedullary nail and plate fixation, have been created to prevent this
complication. These two techniques re-create the medial column of the distal femur.16

Infection
The overall incidence of surgical site infection is approximately 4%, with the rate of deep
infection being approximately 1%.17 The rate of superficial surgical site infection is
approximately 2% to 3%, with Staphylococcus aureus being the most common pathogen.
The rate of S aureus in isolation is 47%, the rate of mixed bacterial infection is 26.7%, and
the rate of S epidermidis is 13.3%.
Periprosthetic Fracture
Placement of plates in the subtrochanteric area can create a stress riser that may contribute to
periprosthetic fracture.
May be observed in patients with osteoporotic femora

Periprosthetic Fracture
During preoperative planning for the management of these fractures, the
subtrochanteric region should be bypassed or the plate should be placed distal to the
subtrochanteric region. The placement of plate or nail constructs in the subtrochanteric
region may increase the risk of subtrochanteric femur fracture.

Incidence: as high as 7% in patients with locking plates18

Retrograde femoral nail
Starting point is paramount
Too posterior of a starting point results in an extension deformity of the distal fracture
segment.
This may especially occur during retrograde nail fixation of periprosthetic fractures as the
knee prosthesis forces a posterior starting point.
Distal femoral plate
If the plate is placed too posterior on the distal femur, it can translate the distal articular
segment medially, creating the golf club deformity
Distal posterior plate positioning also can cause the proximal aspect of the plate to sit too
anterior and off bone. This is especially noticeable with the use of longer plate constructs. If
the plate is placed on the posterior aspect of the distal femur, the proximal aspect of the
plate, because of trajectory, will end up anterior to the shaft.
Symptomatic hardware
Lateral plating may cause irritation of the iliotibial band
Screws that are too long may irritate the medial (screws that are too long from a lateral
locked plate) or lateral soft tissues (screws too long from a retrograde femoral nail). Medial
prominent hardware distal to the epicondyle is particularly poorly tolerated
Knee Instability
Postoperative instability may be related to a ligamentous disruption.
Ligamentous instability should be clinically evaluated after the fractures have been fixed and
before exiting the operating room.
Stiffness
Postoperative stiffness can occur in all patients with a distal femur fracture.
Risks factors include prolonged immobilization, severity of soft-tissue injury, pre-injury
stiffness, and placement of external fixation before definitive fixation.

Management may range from gentle manipulation (early) to formal open release of scar and


Stiffness
Decreased range of motion more commonly occurs in young patients who sustain high-
energy trauma. Other causes include malreduction of the articular surface, intra-
articular hardware, intra-articular adhesions, ligamentous/capsular contractures,
quadriceps or hamstring scarring, or posttraumatic arthritis. After the cause has been
determined, management can proceed. If intra-articular malreduction or hardware is
present, then revision surgery is required to restore the anatomy and remove the
hardware. If intra-articular adhesions are the cause, aggressive physical therapy,
manipulation under anesthesia, or open release may be performed to regain function.7
Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
Deep vein thrombosis may be caused by any factors related to the Virchow triad: stasis, intimal
injury, and hypercoagulable state19
Deep vein thrombosis after distal femur fracture

Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
Zhang et al20 reported a 35% (n = 49) overall incidence of postoperative deep vein
thrombosis, which occurred 5.7 days after open reduction internal fixation. Among the
patients with postoperative deep vein thrombosis, 53.1% (n = 26) and 10.2% (n = 5) were
distal and proximal thromboses, respectively. In addition, the peroneal veins were the
most common sites of deep vein thrombosis (71.4%; n = 35).
